title: Harper v. Commissioner
subject: Business Component Test
summary: Harper v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-57, is a U.S. Tax Court ruling on whether design-build contractors can claim the IRC Section 41 research credit. Denying the IRS's partial summary judgment motion, the Court held that designs, though not "products," could still satisfy the business component test as processes, techniques, or inventions used in the taxpayer's business.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Factual Background and the Taxpayer's Research Credit Claim

In Jeffrey A. Harper and Katherine M. Harper v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, T.C. Memo. 2023-57 (Docket No. 26176-16, filed May 10, 2023), the United States Tax Court addressed a foundational statutory dispute regarding the eligibility of design-build construction and engineering activities for the federal research and development (R&D) tax credit under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). The petitioners, Jeffrey A. Harper and Katherine M. Harper, claimed the credits in connection with the activities of their S corporation, Harper Construction Co. (HCC), which they owned through a grantor trust of which Mr. Harper is the sole grantor and trustee (Mr. Harper is also HCC's president); HCC, founded in 1974 and based in San Diego, California, is a privately owned design builder and general contractor that has worked on residential, commercial, and industrial projects around the country and overseas, and that over the preceding 15 years had specialized in military design-build projects, including over 30 military housing projects.

In 2012, the Harpers engaged a national tax consulting firm, alliantgroup, LP (alliantgroup), to opine on HCC's eligibility for research credits in earlier tax years, and alliantgroup subsequently prepared a separate research credit study for each of the 2012 and 2013 tax years. Those studies were not finalized until after the relevant federal income tax returns had been filed. HCC reported 53 separate projects during the 2012 and 2013 tax years as eligible for the research credit under IRC Section 41—including work on aircraft hangars, maintenance facilities, military recruit barracks and living quarters, college buildings, medical clinics, instructional facilities, fitness centers, parking garages, training facilities, a 200,000-gallon solar-powered water tank, a photovoltaic renewable energy generation system, a multi-megawatt renewable energy system for use in South Africa, and a specialized energy solution in Las Vegas, Nevada. The consulting study calculated "Gross Federal R&D Tax Credits" at the corporate level of $462,168 for 2012 and $387,482 for 2013 (based on total federal QREs, consisting entirely of qualifying wages, of $4,621,679 and $3,874,821, respectively), and described each project as undertaken to develop unique solutions spanning the architectural, civil, structural, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) engineering disciplines, among others. Flowing through from the S corporation, the Harpers claimed net IRC Section 41 research tax credits on their joint individual federal income tax returns of $46,656 for 2012 and $778,610 for 2013, representing an aggregate tax credit claim of $825,266.

Across the 53 claimed projects, HCC operated through a standardized five-phase project delivery lifecycle. The first phase, the job bid phase, involved creating a bid to present to the prospective client. The second phase, conceptual design, encompassed identifying alternatives relating to building materials, building orientation, piping and duct routing, insulation materials, and equipment sizes, and preparing drawings and diagrams of potential project layouts. The third phase, design development, required the preparation of detailed floor plans along with an outline of major building materials, building systems, building code analysis, and methods of implementing the design, with several "submittals" provided to the client at various stages. The fourth phase, documentation, consisted of drafting final permitting packages and construction blueprints. The fifth and final phase, construction, involved physical site execution and facility erection upon securing client and regulatory approvals.

body.text: The Commissioner's Challenge and Procedural Posture

Following an examination of the returns, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed the Harpers' claimed research credits in full and issued a statutory notice of deficiency. After the taxpayers petitioned the United States Tax Court, the Commissioner moved for partial summary judgment, seeking a dispositive legal ruling that HCC's design-build activities failed to satisfy the threshold "business component" requirement of IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and Section 41(d)(2)(B) as a matter of law.

Rather than litigating the granular engineering facts of all 53 projects in its pre-trial motion, the IRS asked the Court to rule that HCC failed the business component test as a matter of law on any one of several alternative grounds. The Commissioner's motion rested on four primary contentions. First, the IRS argued that only the buildings and facilities constructed by HCC (and not the designs HCC created) were "new or improved," and that those structures never belonged to HCC. Second, the IRS contended that HCC's designs were not "products" as that word is intended in the statute, but were instead "tangible manifestations" of construction services. Third, the Commissioner asserted that neither the architectural and engineering designs nor the constructed facilities were "held for sale, lease, or license" by HCC within the meaning of IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)(i). Fourth, the IRS maintained that HCC did not "use" its designs in the sense intended by IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)(ii), because Congress meant for a taxpayer's use of a business component to be "meaningful" and to affect the way a business operates to some degree, and HCC's day-to-day operations were allegedly not changed by its designs.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Harper centers on the statutory architecture of IRC Section 41, which grants a tax credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of a taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over a statutory base amount. Under IRC Section 41(b), QREs comprise in-house research expenses—specifically wages paid to employees engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research, alongside costs of tangible, non-depreciable supplies consumed in research—and 65 percent of eligible contract research expenses paid to third parties.

To generate eligible QREs, the underlying technical activities must satisfy the statutory Four-Part Test codified in IRC Section 41(d)(1) and elaborated in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4. The first requirement, known as the Section 174 Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A), mandates that the expenditures qualify as research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174 (the terminology in effect for the years at issue; the current version of the statute refers to "specified research or experimental expenditures"). Pursuant to Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a), this requires that the costs represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, meaning they are for activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product, a term defined to include any pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property. The second requirement, the Technological in Nature Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i), dictates that the research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the investigative process must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

The third requirement, the Business Component Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), requires that the taxpayer intend the application of the discovered technological information to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Separately, under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Section 41(d)(3)(A), the process of experimentation must relate to a qualified purpose, defined as a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, while Section 41(d)(3)(B) expressly disqualifies research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. The fourth requirement, the Process of Experimentation Test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C), mandates that substantially all—defined under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more on a cost or time basis—of the research activities measured at the business component level constitute elements of a process of experimentation capable of evaluating one or more alternatives through modeling, computational simulation, or systematic trial and error.

Central to the Harper ruling is IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B), which defines a "business component" as "any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be—(i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer." Furthermore, IRC Section 41(d)(2)(A) mandates that the Four-Part Test be applied separately to each discrete business component. If an overall product or project fails to meet the requirements—typically because less than 80 percent of the total project activities constitute experimentation—Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2) provides the "shrinking-back rule," instructing the taxpayer to apply the Four-Part Test to the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention until either a qualifying subset is identified or the most basic element of the activity fails to qualify. Finally, even where the Four-Part Test is satisfied, IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d) exclude "funded research," disqualifying any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity unless the taxpayer both retains substantial rights in the research results and bears the financial risk of technical failure.
The Tax Court's Holding and Statutory Interpretation

In her Memorandum Opinion issued on May 10, 2023, Judge Copeland denied the Commissioner's motion for partial summary judgment, concluding that none of the four alternative grounds advanced by the IRS entitled it to judgment as a matter of law, even though the Court agreed with the IRS that HCC's designs were not "products." Evaluating the record under the summary judgment standard—which requires construing factual materials and drawing all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving taxpayer—the Tax Court held that the Commissioner had failed to establish as a matter of law that HCC's 53 design-build projects could not qualify as statutory business components.

Addressing whether HCC's work was "new or improved," the Tax Court found the Commissioner's contention contradicted by the record, noting that HCC evidently engaged in a lengthy, multistep process of conceptual design and design development for each project that resulted in novel ideas and iterative improvements to them, and reciting sample project descriptions (such as a storm water drainage design, a cockpit air supply system for an aircraft hangar, and energy-efficiency features) that it could not rule out as new or improved. Citing statutory text and judicial precedent, including Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner and Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, Judge Copeland emphasized that, to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component, the research need only provide some level of functional improvement, at a minimum.

The Court next addressed the Commissioner's argument regarding the word "product." While agreeing with the IRS that the term "product" generally denotes a tangible good held for sale and that HCC's engineering drawings and blueprints were not standalone "products," Judge Copeland pointed out that IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) explicitly lists six distinct categories of business components: products, processes, computer software, techniques, formulas, and inventions. Although "designs" are not enumerated verbatim in the statute, the Court concluded that HCC's designs could still potentially constitute processes, techniques, or inventions, so that their failure to qualify as products did not by itself entitle the Commissioner to a ruling that the business component test was not met.

Furthermore, the Court declined to resolve the IRS's argument regarding the ownership of the physical buildings and facilities. As an initial evidentiary matter, the summary judgment record did not contain any of the construction contracts for the projects at issue—the Commissioner had instead extrapolated from HCC's 2008 and 2010 contracts—so the Court could not establish whether HCC ever owned the structures before conveying them to its clients, although it observed that HCC's ownership of buildings constructed on government and private property under a bid process seemed implausible. More fundamentally, Judge Copeland ruled that because a dispute existed as to whether the processes, techniques, and potential inventions HCC developed were used in its business, the Court need not resolve ownership of the buildings and other structures to rule on the motion.

Finally, the Court rejected the IRS's attempt to graft an extratextual "habitual, ongoing, or repeated use" requirement onto IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)(ii). The Commissioner argued, through what the Court described as a conclusory and unevidenced assertion, that HCC's day-to-day operations were not changed by its designs, which the Court took to refer to habitual use. Judge Copeland held that nothing in the plain text of Section 41(d)(2)(B)(ii) requires a business component to be used repeatedly, habitually, or on an ongoing basis. The Court found it indisputable that HCC used its designs—the designs that were permitted and approved before building—in the construction process, in the sense of referring to and relying on them, and declined to accord the word "use" a specialized definition or to look past its plain meaning to the legislative history. Because the record did not permit the Court to rule out that HCC's designs could be processes, techniques, or inventions used in HCC's business, and the Commissioner pointed to no evidence showing that the business component test was not satisfied, the Court denied the motion—noting that the designs "may or may not" run afoul of other restrictions on the credit—and stated that an appropriate order would be issued.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

While Harper v. Commissioner represents a landmark procedural victory that prevented the IRS from categorically barring design-build contractors and A&E firms from the Section 41 credit at the summary judgment stage, the opinion simultaneously exposes severe legal, structural, and evidentiary vulnerabilities in how taxpayers and third-party study providers formulate R&D claims. Understanding why the Harpers' claim was disallowed upon audit, why the Tax Court declined to grant outright credit entitlement, and why other taxpayers with engineering, design, construction, or custom-manufacturing claims have suffered significant defeats—for example in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023) (a shipbuilding case decided by the Tax Court in 2021 and affirmed by the Seventh Circuit before Harper was issued), Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50—requires a rigorous examination of five interconnected compliance failures.
Ambiguous Business Component Classification and Macro-Project Aggregation

The immediate catalyst for the litigation in Harper was the imprecise manner in which HCC and its consulting firm framed the claimed business components across the 53 projects. Rather than isolating specific, functional engineering processes or technical subsystems and mapping them directly to the statutory nouns of IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) (process, technique, or invention), the taxpayer's study broadly characterized whole design-build contracts, architectural drawings, and facility designs as the qualifying business components. This macro-level framing handed the IRS Chief Counsel a direct opening to argue that blueprints and designs are merely the tangible deliverables of professional services rather than statutory "products," and that the physical buildings themselves were owned by the government or commercial clients rather than held for sale by HCC.

Although Judge Copeland rescued the taxpayer from summary disposition by inferring that HCC's conceptual design and design development activities could legally constitute processes, techniques, or inventions used in HCC's construction business, relying on judicial inference at the summary judgment stage is a perilous litigation posture. At trial, where the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proof under Tax Court Rule 142(a), defining a business component as an entire construction project or an overarching "building design" almost invariably fails. A complete military housing complex or training facility comprises thousands of standard, off-the-shelf structural, architectural, and MEP components that involve zero technological uncertainty. When a taxpayer defines the business component at the macro-project level rather than the specific technical process or subsystem level, the denominator of the "substantially all" (80 percent) test expands to encompass every routine hour spent on the contract, mathematically guaranteeing disqualification.
Conflation of Routine Engineering Services with Section 174 Technological Uncertainty

A pervasive technical failure in design-build and A&E claims is the conflation of project complexity and site-specific customization with genuine technological uncertainty under IRC Section 174 and Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2. In Harper, HCC's consulting study stated that each project was undertaken to develop unique solutions spanning architectural, civil, structural, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing engineering, and that HCC faced many uncertainties regarding the final design resulting from the unique combinations of all project requirements. However, in the construction industry, every project begins with uncertainty regarding client budget, site topography, soil bearing capacity, local zoning codes, and spatial layout. Resolving these project-specific variables through standard engineering calculations, code lookups, or professional experience does not satisfy Section 174.

Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(3), technological uncertainty exists only if the information available to the taxpayer at the outset of the research does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that component. Furthermore, IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B) strictly excludes any design work related to aesthetic, style, taste, or cosmetic factors. In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2024-113)—a later MEP engineering case decided on December 23, 2024—the Tax Court examined three sample building projects (including a military psychiatric unit, a hospital, and a university science building) that followed a multi-stage design process virtually identical to HCC's five-phase workflow. The Tax Court disallowed the credits in full and upheld accuracy-related penalties because the engineering firm failed to prove that the information available to it did not already establish the appropriate design, or how technical uncertainty in a single MEP element created functional uncertainty across the broader system. Similarly, in Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-84), the Tax Court rejected claims for custom-built industrial oxidizers because the taxpayer failed to demonstrate that the custom units were "pilot models" constructed to resolve genuine design uncertainty rather than commercial units engineered using known scientific principles.
Deficiencies in the Process of Experimentation and Shrinking-Back Misapplication

Even where genuine Section 174 uncertainty exists at the outset of a conceptual design phase, taxpayers routinely fail to prove that "substantially all" (80 percent or more) of the activities constituted elements of a structured process of experimentation under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C). In Harper, HCC's operational model spanned five distinct phases: (1) Job bid, (2) Conceptual design, (3) Design development, (4) Documentation (permitting and construction plans), and (5) Construction. When a taxpayer sweeps wage and subcontractor costs from Phase 1 (bidding and client proposals), Phase 4 (routine CAD drafting and municipal permitting), and Phase 5 (physical construction execution and routine site supervision) into the R&D claim, those non-experimental activities overwhelm the calculation.

As established by the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and reinforced by the Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group, the 80 percent "substantially all" fraction requires rigorous arithmetic substantiation. While direct supervision and direct support of experimental activities are not categorically excluded from the numerator provided their nexus to experimentation is proven, general project administration, routine drafting, code compliance verification, and standard construction quality control must be placed in the denominator (if part of the defined component's development) or excluded entirely.

Crucially, taxpayers frequently misunderstand how the "shrinking-back rule" of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2) operates when a macro-project fails the 80 percent test. In Phoenix Design Group, the taxpayer attempted to rescue its claim by arguing that if an entire building's MEPF system failed the Four-Part Test, the Court should "shrink back" either to a specific design phase (such as the schematic or design development phase) or to the activities of specific senior engineers. The Tax Court flatly rejected this methodology, holding that the shrinking-back rule applies strictly to a smaller subset of elements of the physical or functional business component (for example, shrinking back from an entire building to the electrical system, and then to an emergency power generation technique), and can never be used to shrink back to a chronological project phase or to individual employees' tasks. Because the Harper opinion describes HCC's work in terms of five chronological stages across 53 projects, and HCC's studies described each project as a whole rather than isolating discrete sub-component processes (the opinion does not address how HCC tracked time), HCC would have faced this exact evidentiary barrier had the case proceeded to trial on these issues.
Retroactive Study Methodology and Insufficient Contemporaneous Substantiation

A major evidentiary weakness reflected in the Harper record is the timing of the taxpayer's R&D studies. The Harpers retained alliantgroup in 2012 to opine on HCC's eligibility in earlier tax years, and the research credit studies for 2012 and 2013 were not finalized until after the relevant tax returns had been filed; the opinion does not describe the methodology the studies used. Furthermore, the opinion reports, without explaining the difference, both the consulting study's "Gross Federal R&D Tax Credits" ($462,168 for 2012 and $387,482 for 2013) and the credits claimed on the Harpers' tax returns ($46,656 for 2012 and $778,610 for 2013).

Federal courts have grown increasingly hostile to retroactive R&D studies that apply high-level percentage estimates to employee W-2 wages without contemporaneous documentation linking specific hours and supplies to specific business components and experimental iterations. In Phoenix Design Group, Betz, and Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20), the Tax Court denied credits where timesheets merely recorded generic project numbers or phases without distinguishing experimental modeling from routine drafting or executive oversight. To enforce this standard administratively, the IRS issued its Chief Counsel Memorandum on Section 41 refund claims and overhauled Form 6765 (specifically introducing Section G), mandating that taxpayers contemporaneously identify for every claimed business component its unique alphanumeric identifier, component type (product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention), all research activities performed, the specific individuals performing them, the exact technical information sought to be discovered, and the direct reconciliation of wage, supply, and contract research QREs to each component.
Contractual Exposure Under the Funded Research Exclusion

Although the summary judgment record in Harper did not contain any of HCC's construction contracts for the projects at issue (the Commissioner relied instead on extrapolation from HCC's 2008 and 2010 contracts to argue ownership), and the funded research exclusion was not before the Court on the motion, the funded research exclusion under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d) represents an existential threat to any design-build or military contractor proceeding to trial. Under the two-prong regulatory standard established in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), research performed under a third-party or government contract is disqualified as "funded" unless the taxpayer proves both: (1) that payment is contingent on the technical success of the research (the financial risk test), and (2) that the taxpayer retains "substantial rights" in the research results.

Almost exactly one year after Harper, on May 6, 2024, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals issued its pivotal ruling in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), affirming the Tax Court's disallowance of R&D credits for a structural engineering firm. Even assuming MBJ's structural designs satisfied the Business Component Test under Harper, the Eighth Circuit held that MBJ's fixed-price and milestone-based contracts were fully "funded" because payment was tied to the delivery of professional engineering services and adherence to standard professional care rather than contingent on the successful resolution of technical research uncertainties. Similarly, in Grigsby v. United States (5th Cir. 2023) and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (decided June 16, 2026), the courts emphasized that fixed-price construction or architectural contracts are not inherently unfunded simply because the contractor faces the economic risk of cost overruns; rather, the contract must contain explicit technical performance specifications and rejection/refund remedies under governing law (as noted in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21) that condition the client's obligation to pay on successful research outcomes. Furthermore, for military design-build contractors like HCC, standard Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) and Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) clauses frequently vest unlimited rights or exclusive ownership of technical data in the federal government, stripping the contractor of "substantial rights" unless the contract is carefully structured to carve out background and foreground construction processes and engineering techniques.
Comparative Summary of Statutory Requirements, Litigation Pitfalls, and Judicial Standards of Proof

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement implicated in Harper v. Commissioner and related federal Tax Court jurisprudence against the specific legal or evidentiary deficiencies that trigger IRS disallowance and the governing judicial standard of proof required to prevail at trial.

cells: Business Component Identification IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii); IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)

Taxpayers and study consultants loosely label whole construction projects, buildings, or blueprint "designs" as the business component. The IRS challenges "designs" as non-statutory tangible representations of services and argues that the physical buildings are not owned by the contractor.

While "designs" are not "products," Judge Copeland held in Harper that engineering designs could potentially constitute a statutory process, technique, or invention, so the IRS was not entitled to summary judgment. At trial, the taxpayer must precisely identify the discrete process, technique, or invention rather than aggregating the entire facility.
New or Improved Functional Purpose IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii); IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)-(B)
Taxpayers claim routine site adaptations, architectural floor plan layouts, or aesthetic/cosmetic client preferences as "new or improved" components without quantifying functional metrics.

Under Harper (citing Norwest), the research need only provide some level of functional improvement, at a minimum, to be useful in developing a new or improved business component. However, the taxpayer must provide objective technical evidence distinguishing functional engineering enhancements from excluded aesthetic, style, or routine code-compliance work.
"Held for Sale" vs. "Used in Trade or Business" IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)(i)-(ii)

The IRS argues that designs are not "held for sale" and fail the "used in a trade or business" prong because the taxpayer's use was not "meaningful," asserting that the contractor's day-to-day operations were not changed by its designs.

Harper explicitly rejected the IRS's attempt to read a "habitual" use requirement into the statute. The statute requires only that the process, technique, or invention be used by the taxpayer in its trade or business; the Court found it indisputable that HCC used its designs in the construction process by referring to and relying on them.
Elimination of Technical Uncertainty IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); IRC § 174; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)

Taxpayers conflate business, scheduling, or site-discovery uncertainty with technological uncertainty, failing to prove why standard engineering calculations or publicly available knowledge could not establish the appropriate design.

The taxpayer must prove through contemporaneous records that information available at the outset of the project did not establish the capability, method, or appropriate final design of the specific business component, and must demonstrate how component-level uncertainty impacted system performance (Phoenix Design Group; Betz).
Process of Experimentation & "Substantially All" (80%) Rule IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)-(6)

Taxpayers bundle all project lifecycle phases—such as HCC's Phase 1 (Job Bid), Phase 4 (Permitting/Documentation), and Phase 5 (Construction)—into the claim, diluting experimental activities well below the mandatory 80% threshold.

Under Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group, the taxpayer must arithmetically prove that at least 80% of the activities (by cost or time) applied to the specific business component constituted elements of a structured process of experimentation (evaluating alternatives via modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error) or direct supervision/support thereof.
Application of the Shrinking-Back Rule IRC § 41(d)(2)(A); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)
When a whole building or MEP system fails the 80% test, taxpayers attempt to "shrink back" to a chronological design phase (e.g., Conceptual Design) or to the hours of specific engineers.

As established in Phoenix Design Group, shrinking back cannot be applied to a project phase or to specific employees. The taxpayer must shrink back strictly to a discrete physical or functional subset of the business component (e.g., a specialized structural foundation process) and substantiate both experimentation and isolated QREs at that subset level.
QRE Nexus & Contemporaneous Documentation IRC § 41(b); IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d)
Reliance on post-filing consulting studies (like HCC's studies, which were not finalized until after the returns were filed) that do not tie hours to discrete components.

Taxpayers cannot rely on high-level retroactive estimates or the Cohan rule without a credible evidentiary foundation. Records must establish a direct nexus between specific employee wages, supplies, or subcontractors and the lowest-level qualifying business component, satisfying IRS Form 6765 Section G granularity.
Funded Research Exclusion (Financial Risk & Substantial Rights) IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)

Executing design-build or A&E work under standard fixed-price or milestone contracts where payment is made for professional services rendered, or where FAR/DFARS/client IP clauses strip the contractor of rights to reuse the developed techniques.

Under Fairchild Industries, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Smith, the taxpayer must prove via express contract terms and governing state/federal law that: (1) payment is contingent on the technical success of the research (subject to rejection/refund for failing strict technical specifications), and (2) the taxpayer retains substantial rights to use the developed processes/techniques without paying royalties.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how taxpayers in the construction, engineering, and custom manufacturing sectors can operationalize the legal holdings of Harper v. Commissioner while insulating their claims against the trial-level disqualifications seen in Phoenix Design Group, Little Sandy Coal, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Smith, the following two industry case studies detail a step-by-step remedial compliance architecture.
Case Study 1: Military Design-Build Contractor Developing Blast-Resistant Modular Structural Systems
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

Aegis Defense Constructors, Inc. (ADC), a domestic S corporation operating as a prime design-build contractor, is awarded a $45 million contract by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to design and construct a specialized Live-Fire Urban Breach and Munitions Testing Facility at a military installation. The facility requires interior structural walls and blast-containment baffles capable of withstanding repeated close-proximity C-4 demolitions without spalling or structural fatigue, while simultaneously integrating rapid-reconfiguration modular wall tracks.

Mirroring the operational workflow in Harper, ADC executes the contract across five internal stages: (1) Bid Proposal, (2) Conceptual Design, (3) Design Development, (4) Permitting/Construction Documentation, and (5) Field Construction. After filing its tax return, ADC hires an R&D provider that defines the entire "Live-Fire Urban Breach Facility Design" as a single business component, claims 60 percent of the wages of all project managers, structural engineers, CAD drafters, and site superintendents across all five phases based on oral interviews, and ignores the underlying USACE contract terms. Upon IRS examination, the claim faces total disallowance on four grounds: defining the entire facility design as the business component fails the 80 percent "substantially all" test because Phases 1, 4, and 5 consist of routine bidding, blueprint drafting, and conventional concrete pouring; attempting to shrink back to "Phase 2 and Phase 3 Design Activities" is legally invalid under Phoenix Design Group; the lack of sub-component time tracking prevents isolating QREs; and the standard USACE milestone payment schedule and DFARS technical data clauses trigger the funded research exclusion under Meyer, Borgman & Johnson.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Business Component Isolation Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)

To capitalize on Judge Copeland's holding in Harper while avoiding macro-project dilution, ADC's tax and engineering governance committee must restructure how projects are initialized in the company's Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system prior to commencing conceptual design. ADC must abandon claiming the "Facility Design" as a product and instead establish two discrete, lowest-level business components classified expressly as a process and a technique used in ADC's design-build trade or business under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)(ii). Specifically, ADC designates Business Component BC-2026-01 (Process) as its Proprietary Ultra-High-Performance Fiber-Reinforced Concrete (UHPFRC) Field-Curing and Pneumatic Placement Process for Zero-Spall Blast Walls, and designates Business Component BC-2026-02 (Technique) as its Kinetic Energy-Absorbing Elastomeric Isolation Joint Technique for Modular Live-Fire Tracks. By isolating these two specific technical processes and techniques from the remaining 90 percent of the facility—such as the building foundation, standard roofing, administrative offices, and parking lots—ADC ensures that the Four-Part Test is applied strictly to the novel engineering subsets in accordance with IRC Section 41(d)(2)(A) and the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2).
Step 2: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation of Section 174 Uncertainty

At project inception, ADC's Lead Structural Engineer must author a formal Technical Uncertainty and Baseline Knowledge Charter for both BC-2026-01 and BC-2026-02. Rather than citing general project complexity, the charter must document why publicly available USACE Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC 3-340-02) and standard ACI structural codes cannot establish the appropriate design or method. Specifically, the charter records that standard steel-reinforced concrete spalls violently under repeated sub-3-meter charges, while conventional UHPFRC mixes suffer from thermal micro-cracking when poured pneumatically in thicknesses exceeding 18 inches in arid field conditions. This contemporaneous record proves that the capability, method, and appropriate design of the field-curing process and isolation joint technique were technologically uncertain at the outset.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring to Overcome the Funded Research Exclusion

To prevent disqualification under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, ADC's legal counsel must structure the design-build contract and its Contract Line Item Numbers (CLINs) to satisfy both prongs of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d). To establish financial risk where payment is contingent on technical success, ADC negotiates a dedicated fixed-price CLIN for the blast-containment subsystem that incorporates strict, objective technical performance acceptance criteria modeled on Fairchild Industries. The contract stipulates that payment for this CLIN, as well as the retention of any progress advances, is expressly contingent upon the constructed pilot wall assembly surviving a mandatory live-fire qualification test consisting of 50 consecutive 2.5-kilogram C-4 detonations at 1.5 meters with zero rear-face spalling and track deflection under 2.0 millimeters. The contract explicitly states that if ADC's engineering process fails to achieve this technical benchmark, USACE has the absolute right to reject the subsystem, withhold payment, and demand a full refund of any milestone advances paid under that CLIN, without limitation to mere repair-or-replace warranty remedies.

Simultaneously, to satisfy the substantial rights retention prong, ADC structures the intellectual property provisions to distinguish the physical real estate from the contractor's operational methods. While the federal government takes title to the physical building and retains standard DFARS rights in the facility's as-built maintenance blueprints, ADC includes an explicit intellectual property addendum under DFARS 252.227-7013 and 252.227-7015 confirming that the underlying UHPFRC placement process (BC-2026-01) and kinetic isolation joint engineering technique (BC-2026-02) constitute ADC's proprietary trade secrets and construction methods. Consequently, ADC retains the unfettered, royalty-free right to deploy these processes and techniques on all future military and commercial design-build contracts.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and QRE Substantiation Architecture

To satisfy the 80 percent "substantially all" math required by Little Sandy Coal and the reporting mandates of IRS Form 6765 Section G, ADC reconfigures its timekeeping and job-costing ledger. Employees are prohibited from charging R&D codes during Phase 1 (Job Bid), Phase 4 (Routine Permitting/Blueprint Drafting), or general Phase 5 (Standard Construction). Instead, ADC opens dedicated sub-job cost codes (2026-01-EXP and 2026-02-EXP) restricted exclusively to the iterative hypothesis formulation, finite element analysis (FEA) blast simulations using LS-DYNA software, laboratory batch mixing of three alternative steel and polypropylene fiber ratios, and destructive field testing of three prototype blast panels. Every time entry requires a mandatory 150-character technical log noting the specific alternative evaluated and the test parameter measured, ensuring that over 92 percent of the hours logged to BC-2026-01 and BC-2026-02 represent direct experimentation, direct technical supervision, or direct fabrication support of the test panels.

body.text: Case Study 2: Multidisciplinary MEP Engineering Firm Designing High-Containment Clinical HVAC and Energy Recovery Processes
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

Vanguard MEP Engineers, LLP (Vanguard), a multidisciplinary mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) engineering firm taxed as a partnership, enters into a contract with a regional university medical center to engineer the mechanical and air-handling systems for a new Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) Infectious Disease Research Pavilion. The facility requires 100 percent outside air intake with zero cross-contamination between negative-pressure isolation suites, while simultaneously meeting a strict municipal mandate to reduce thermal energy consumption by 40 percent compared to standard ASHRAE 90.1 hospital baselines.

Operating under a standard American Institute of Architects (AIA) consultant agreement, Vanguard follows a six-stage design process identical to the taxpayer in Phoenix Design Group: Program Verification, Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Bidding/Negotiation, and Construction Administration. Vanguard claims Section 41 credits for the entire "BSL-3 Pavilion MEP System Design," relying on generic timesheets where engineers log hours simply to "Project #408 - Schematic Design" and "Project #408 - Design Development." When challenged by the IRS that less than 80 percent of the total MEP project hours involved experimentation, Vanguard argues that the Court should "shrink back" to the Schematic Design phase or to the hours of its two Principal Mechanical Engineers. Moreover, Vanguard's AIA contract provides for monthly progress payments based on the percentage of completion of engineering drawings and grants the university ownership of all instruments of service upon payment. Under Phoenix Design Group, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Smith, Vanguard's claim faces complete disqualification and accuracy-related penalties under IRC Section 6662.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Shrinking-Back Alignment and Granular Business Component Isolation

Vanguard's tax advisory team must immediately eliminate the practice of claiming whole-building MEP systems or attempting to shrink back to chronological design phases (such as Schematic Design) or specific employee classifications. Applying the Harper holding that a taxpayer's engineering designs could potentially qualify as a process, technique, or invention used in the taxpayer's trade or business under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)(ii), alongside the Phoenix Design Group rule that shrinking back applies solely to functional subsets of a component, Vanguard isolates one highly specific engineering technique as its sole business component on the project. Vanguard formally designates Business Component VM-2026-09 (Technique) as its Dual-Loop Run-Around Coil Enthalpy Recovery and UV-C Photolytic Purge Technique for Negative-Pressure BSL-3 Exhaust Plenums. All routine MEP engineering for the pavilion—including standard domestic plumbing, fire sprinkler layouts, normal office VAV boxes, lighting fixtures, and main electrical switchgear—is segregated into non-qualifying project codes at the outset.
Step 2: Establishing Component-Level Technical Uncertainty and System Interaction

In Phoenix Design Group, the Tax Court faulted the taxpayer for failing to show how uncertainty in a single MEP element created technical uncertainty across the system, and for relying on standard engineering calculations. To cure this defect, Vanguard's Principal Mechanical Engineer documents a pre-design Technical Uncertainty Analysis for VM-2026-09. The analysis demonstrates that standard enthalpy wheels are prohibited in BSL-3 exhaust streams due to aerosol carry-over risks, whereas conventional run-around glycol coils freeze under winter intake temperatures when attempting to capture the heat required to meet the 40 percent energy reduction target without restricting the negative-pressure static head required for pathogen containment. Consequently, the exact coil geometry, variable-flow glycol modulation algorithm, and aerodynamic baffle placement within the UV-C kill zone cannot be established using published ASHRAE handbooks or standard psychrometric tables, establishing genuine Section 174 uncertainty regarding capability and appropriate design.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring for Unfunded Research and IP Carve-Outs

Because standard AIA progress-payment contracts fail the financial risk test under Meyer, Borgman & Johnson and Smith, Vanguard executes a bilateral Special Research and Performance Addendum to its engineering agreement prior to commencing work on the BSL-3 exhaust recovery subsystem. To establish contingent payment and an enforceable rejection remedy, the addendum carves out a $350,000 fixed fee specifically for the engineering of the Dual-Loop BSL-3 Exhaust Energy Recovery Technique (VM-2026-09). Payment of this fee, as well as the right to retain any interim draws, is expressly conditioned upon the final engineered subsystem passing third-party commissioning verification demonstrating three concurrent benchmarks: a 0.0001 percent maximum tracer-gas cross-leakage at 150 Pascals negative pressure, zero coil frost accumulation at -15°C ambient intake, and a minimum 42 percent sensible and latent thermal recovery efficiency. Under the addendum and governing state contract law, if the engineered technique fails to achieve these three numerical parameters during commissioning, the university is entitled to reject the design deliverable and receive a 100 percent refund of all fees paid under the addendum, establishing genuine financial risk of research failure.

To preserve substantial rights in the research results, the addendum simultaneously modifies the standard AIA "Instruments of Service" clause. The modified covenant specifies that while the university receives a non-exclusive license to operate the physical HVAC system at the pavilion, Vanguard retains sole ownership and substantial rights in the underlying engineering technique, CFD models, and thermodynamic control logic (VM-2026-09), with the unrestricted right to deploy the technique across future healthcare and laboratory clients without paying royalties or seeking university consent.
Step 4: Structured Computational Experimentation and Time-Tracking Hygiene

To satisfy the Process of Experimentation test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and the 80 percent rule of Little Sandy Coal, Vanguard implements a strict time-and-version-control protocol linking its Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) platforms (ANSYS Fluent and Revit) directly to its accounting ledger. Engineers charge time to code VM-2026-09-POE only when executing structured experimental cycles evaluating competing technical alternatives. In the first experimental cycle (Iterations 1.1 through 1.4), the engineering team models a counter-flow micro-channel glycol coil array with high-turbulence louver baffles, which is subsequently rejected after ANSYS CFD simulation reveals localized pressure drops exceeding fan static limits and creating dead-air pockets in the UV-C irradiation chamber. In the second experimental cycle (Iterations 2.1 through 2.6), the team formulates and models a three-stage split-loop glycol-water-glycol heat pipe geometry with Pulsed-Width Modulated (PWM) bypass valves and parabolic UV-C reflectors, which is validated via transient thermal-fluid simulation to achieve 43.2 percent energy recovery with zero frost formation at -18°C.

Each simulation run generates an automated timestamped revision log in ANSYS Fluent that cross-references the exact hours logged by the mechanical engineers and their direct technical supervisor on their daily timesheets. Once Iteration 2.6 is validated and frozen, all subsequent hours spent generating 2D construction blueprints, writing standard equipment specifications, reviewing contractor shop drawings, and performing site walk-throughs are logged to a separate, non-qualifying code (VM-2026-09-ADMIN), ensuring that 100 percent of the hours captured in the R&D numerator and denominator for component VM-2026-09 represent pure experimental activities.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions for Federal R&D Tax Credit Practice

The United States Tax Court's decision in Harper v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-57, establishes an essential statutory shield for taxpayers operating in design-build construction, architectural engineering, and custom manufacturing. By denying the Commissioner's motion for partial summary judgment, Judge Copeland articulated two vital principles: first, that although custom construction designs are not tangible "products," they could potentially constitute new or improved processes, techniques, or inventions under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B), so their failure to qualify as products does not by itself defeat the business component test; and second, that the statutory requirement that a business component be "used by the taxpayer in a trade or business" under Section 41(d)(2)(B)(ii) carries its plain meaning and does not require habitual use, with the Court finding it indisputable that HCC used its designs in the construction process by referring to and relying on them.

Nevertheless, tax practitioners and corporate tax directors must recognize that Harper resolved only a threshold legal defense at the partial summary judgment stage and did not validate the taxpayer's underlying evidentiary methodology. When read in concert with the Tax Court's subsequent trial rulings in Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), Betz (T.C. Memo. 2023-84), and Smith (T.C. Memo. 2026-50), alongside appellate precedent in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287) and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (100 F.4th 986), a clear doctrinal boundary emerges. Taxpayers who rely on post-filing studies that aggregate entire construction projects, conflate chronological design phases with statutory business components, apply blanket percentage allocations to employee wages, or operate under standard service contracts lacking contingent technical acceptance criteria and IP retention clauses will face total disallowance and accuracy-related penalties at trial. Sustaining a federal research credit claim under IRC Section 41 requires proactive, pre-project legal and technical governance that isolates discrete processes and techniques at the lowest functional subset, embeds explicit technical performance contingencies and IP carve-outs into client contracts, and captures contemporaneous, iteration-level experimentation records aligned with the granular reporting standards of IRS Form 6765 Section G.

metaDescription: Harper v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-57, is a U.S. Tax Court ruling on whether design-build contractors can claim the IRC Section 41 research credit.
